A quick reference to the exported names. Every function below has a docstring you
can reach with ?name at the REPL.

DatabaseConfig(; dbname, user, host = "localhost", port = 5432, password = nothing,
                 sslmode = "prefer", connect_timeout = 10, readpoolsize = 8,
                 max_batch = 1, failure = :abort, retries = nothing, retry_time = nothing,
                 retry_delay = 0.1, retry_delay_max = 5.0, on_error = nothing,
                 conninfo = nothing)
DatabaseConfig(url::AbstractString; kwargs...)

create_database(config; overwrite = false) -> Database
open_database(config)                      -> Database
MemoryDatabase()                           -> MemoryDatabase   # fake, in-memory, for tests
Base.close(db::Database)

AirDB.sync(db::Database)                   # wait until queued writes are saved
AirDB.status(db::Database)                 # (npending, last_error)
pending_writes(db::Database)               # the writer's unsaved updates

DatabaseConfig field

meaning

read connections to keep

max_batch

commits accumulated before one database write

failure

:abort or :retry

retry budget: attempts and/or seconds

backoff between retries

on_error(db, err) hook called on every database error

Form(x::FormLeaf)           # a scalar form from one leaf
Form(seq, map)              # a container from prepared collections
form(seq...; keys...)       # the general builder
form()                      # an empty container
to_form(x)                  # convert any value to a form
value(fs)                   # the leaf a scalar form wraps

length(f); isempty(f)       # collection protocol, in the canonical order
keys(f); values(f); pairs(f)
first(f); last(f); copy(f); empty(f)

update(f, fn, idxs...)      # read-modify-write
update!(f, fn, idxs...)     # ... transactional (deepest volatile, like setindex!)
merge(f, g, ...)            # combine: sequences concat, maps merge (later wins)
merge_with(fn, f, g)        # ... combining shared keys with fn
haskey(f, idxs...)          # does the path resolve?
select_keys(f, ks)          # a form with only these keys
filter(pred, f); map_values(fn, f); map_keys(fn, f); deep_map(fn, f)
to_vector(f); to_dict(f)    # convert out to ordinary Julia data

hold(f); unhold(f)          # the `held` flag (containers, symbol scalars)
isheld(f)

Reading and updating use ordinary indexing; see


Indexing and updating.f[idxs...]                  # getindex / get along a path
get(f, idxs..., default)
setindex(f, v, idxs...)     # functional update (returns a new form)
setindex!(f, v, idxs...)    # transactional update (writes a volatile; needs @tx)
map(fn, f)                  # elementwise, keys preserved

push(f, v); pop(f); delete(f, k)
length(f); haskey(f, k)

VolatileForm(db, seq...; keys...) -> VolatileForm
VolatileForm(db, form::Form)      -> VolatileForm
get_form(db, id::UUID)            -> VolatileForm
isloaded(vf)                      -> Bool
AirDB.load!(vf)                   -> VolatileForm

vf[]                              # read the whole form (loads if needed)
vf[idxs...]                       # read along a path

named_form(db, name; create = false, value = nothing)  # look up, or create, by name
name_form!(db, name, vf::VolatileForm)                 # register vf under name (overwrites)
named_forms(db)                                        # the whole table, as a PDict

name may be a Symbol or a String; both refer to the same form. For
named_form, create is false (raise if absent), true (create; raise if
present), or nothing (return nothing if absent). value is the new form’s
initial value, used only when creating; it may be a Form, something a Form can
be made from, nothing (an empty form), or an existing VolatileForm (which is
aliased rather than copied). Registering or renaming is transactional: it joins
the caller’s transaction, or runs in one of its own.

AirDB.to_JSON(f::Form)              -> String
AirDB.from_JSON(s)                  -> Form            # no volatile links
AirDB.from_JSON(resolve, s)         -> Form            # resolve "@<uuid>" links
AirDB.from_JSON(db, s)              -> Form            # resolve links via the database

AbstractAirExtern                   # supertype of a host-level value a form can hold
FormExtern(x)                       # the form wrapping one
value(fe)                           # the extern back out

serialize_extern(obj)               # provider: obj -> JSON-able payload (a method)
deserialize_extern(::Val{name}, p)  # provider: payload -> obj (a method)
register_extern(:name, T;           # register T under a symbol, with its equality
                isequal = ===,      #   (a function, not a method: no piracy)

See 

Extern types.
AirDB builds on Air’s transaction system, which you use directly:using Air                  # @tx, tx, Volatile, Actor, send, ...

error

raised when

ArgumentError

a bad config, a non-key index, no volatile on a setindex! path, indexing a leaf

KeyError

a missing map key

BoundsError

a missing sequence position, or an out-of-range append

FormNotFound

loading a form whose id is not in the database

DatabaseError

a database operation failed and the policy gave up

ExternError

a form holds an extern type that is not registered

ExternTombstone

an extern was written as a tombstone (:abandoned/:expired)

AirDB is built for many threads sharing data. The model is simple: many readers
and writers, one writer actor.

Reads go through a pool of connections and never wait on the writer. Writes are
dispatched to a single writer actor in Air’s global commit order, so the database
sees transactions in exactly the order they committed — no deadlocks, no
row-level lock contention, no two writers racing.counter = VolatileForm(db, n = 0)
AirDB.sync(db)

@sync for _ in 1:50
    Threads.@spawn tx(() -> (counter[:n] = value(counter[:n]) + 1))
end
AirDB.sync(db)

value(counter[:n])                 # 50 — every increment committed exactly once

Under contention Air re-runs transactions that lose a race, so the final value
is correct even though the bodies run more than once. The history reflects only
the commits that succeeded, one row each.# form_history has one new row per successful commit, versions in order

Run Julia with more than one thread to see real contention:JULIA_NUM_THREADS=4 julia --project=. examples/quickstart.jl

get_form returns the same object for a given id as long as it is alive, no
matter which thread asks, so two threads that hold a form share its value and its
transactional identity.id = ...
results = Vector{VolatileForm}(undef, 16)
@sync for i in 1:16
    Threads.@spawn (results[i] = get_form(db, id))
end
all(r -> r === results[1], results)   # true

A form queued for a write is held by the writer’s queue until the write succeeds,
so it cannot be collected — and reloaded from the database — while a write that
updates it is pending. This is why read-your-writes holds even under batching and
concurrency: a form with an unsaved change is always still in memory.

Do not read a form and then write it outside a transaction: reads are
always safe, but a write must be inside @tx, and a read-modify-write must be
inside a single transaction to be atomic.

Do not put side effects in a transaction body: it may run more than once.# Atomic read-modify-write: correct.
@tx counter[:n] = value(counter[:n]) + 1

# Not atomic: another thread may interleave between the read and the write.
n = value(counter[:n])
@tx counter[:n] = n + 1

A form holds leaves and other forms — everything JSON can say. But a running
program also holds things JSON cannot: a promise, an open socket, a handle to a
configuration cache, a resolved future. These are externs, and a form holds
one inside a FormExtern.

An extern type subclasses AbstractAirExtern, and its provider teaches AirDB how
to store it: serialize_extern turns one into JSON-able data, and
deserialize_extern turns that data back. The type is registered under a symbol,
which is what appears in the database.using AirDB
# `serialize_extern` and `deserialize_extern` are methods of AirDB's functions, so
# a provider `import`s them and defines methods unqualified.
import AirDB: serialize_extern, deserialize_extern

struct ConfigHandle <: AbstractAirExtern
    version::Int
    label::String
end

serialize_extern(c::ConfigHandle) = Dict("version" => c.version, "label" => c.label)
deserialize_extern(::Val{:config}, p::AbstractDict) =
    ConfigHandle(Int(p[:version]), String(p[:label]))

register_extern(:config, ConfigHandle;
                isequal = (a, b) -> a.version == b.version && a.label == b.label,
                hash = (x, h) -> hash(x.version, hash(x.label, h)))

Now a ConfigHandle is a value a form can hold, alongside any leaf or nested
form:f = form(1, cfg = ConfigHandle(2, "abc"))
f[:cfg]                # FormExtern(ConfigHandle(2, "abc"))
value(f[:cfg])         # ConfigHandle(2, "abc")

to_form(x) wraps any AbstractAirExtern in a FormExtern, and value unwraps
it — the same pair that works for a scalar form.

An extern is written as a tagged list, ["extern", "<type>", <payload>], where the
tag is the string extern, the type is the name it was registered under, and the
payload is what serialize_extern returned. A list whose first element is the tag
string is an extern; a list whose first element is a list is a container, so
the two never collide.using AirDB: to_JSON, from_JSON

to_JSON(FormExtern(ConfigHandle(2, "abc")))
# "[\"'extern\", \":config\", [[], {\":label\": \"'abc\", \":version\": 2}, false]]"

from_JSON("[\"'extern\", \":config\", [[], {\":label\": \"'abc\", \":version\": 2}, false]]")
# FormExtern(ConfigHandle(2, "abc"))

A scalar payload is written as its bare leaf, so an extern that serializes to one
value is compact:to_JSON(FormExtern(OpaqueHandle(7)))     # "[\"'extern\", \":opaque\", 7]"

Reading an extern dispatches on the name in the registry: the reader looks it up
and calls deserialize_extern(Val(name), payload). The payload is ordinary Julia
data — a leaf, a Vector, a Dict — because an extern is not required to
serialize as a form.

An extern that stands for something active — an unresolved promise, an open
socket — cannot be persisted, and should say so rather than fail. The convention
is a tombstone: return the symbol :abandoned (or :expired).serialize_extern(p::Promise) = isready(p) ? fetch(p) : :abandoned

A tombstone is written like any other payload, but reading it back raises
ExternTombstone instead of calling the provider — the value is gone, and the
caller is told so plainly:from_JSON("[\"'extern\", \":promise\", \":abandoned\"]")
# ERROR: the extern :promise was written as a tombstone (:abandoned) and cannot be rehydrated

serialize_extern runs on the database’s writer thread while the committed form
is encoded, so it must not block: an extern that is not ready should return a
tombstone, not wait for a value.

Two FormExterns are equal only if they wrap the same object — identity — unless
the provider registered something else. Because a provider cannot extend == for
AirDB’s FormExtern wrapper without committing type piracy, the comparison is a
function supplied at registration, as in the example above. isequal and hash
must agree — equal externs must hash equal — so give both or neither. With
neither, an extern compares by identity, which is the right default for a live
handle.

error

raised when

ExternError

a form holds an extern type that is not registered, on write or on read

ExternTombstone

a form is read back and its extern was written as a tombstone

A connection to PostgreSQL can fail at any time — a dropped socket, a restart, a
network blip. AirDB gives you two policies, chosen with failure on the
DatabaseConfig.

As soon as a database operation fails, the database is failed: the writer
actor is poisoned, every later write raises, and every later read raises. Nothing
is silently lost, but the database is unusable until it is replaced.db = create_database(DatabaseConfig(; dbname = "airdb_test", user = "airdb");
                     overwrite = true)
vf = VolatileForm(db, n = 1)
AirDB.sync(db)

close(db.writeactor[].conn)      # break the writer connection
@tx vf[:n] = 2
AirDB.sync(db)
# ERROR: AirDB database error: ... (1 unsaved write(s))

db.failure isa DatabaseError     # true
get_form(db, uuid4())[]          # ERROR: AirDB database error: ...

With failure = :retry, a failed operation is retried instead, reconnecting
first, while a budget lasts. Reads block until a retry succeeds (or the budget
is spent); writes accumulate in the writer’s queue meanwhile.cfg = DatabaseConfig(;
    dbname     = "airdb_test",
    user       = "airdb",
    failure    = :retry,
    retries    = 5,          # retry at most 5 times ...
    retry_time = 30.0,       # ... or for at most 30 seconds (whichever first)
    retry_delay = 0.1,       # wait 0.1 s before the first retry ...
    retry_delay_max = 5.0,   # ... doubling up to 5 s between attempts
)
db = create_database(cfg; overwrite = true)

vf = VolatileForm(db, n = 1)
AirDB.sync(db)
close(db.writeactor[].conn)      # break the writer connection
@tx vf[:n] = 2
AirDB.sync(db)                   # the writer reconnects, retries, and succeeds
vf[:n]                           # 2
db.failure === nothing           # true — the database is healthy

You give a budget as a number of retries (retries), an amount of time
(retry_time), or both — whichever runs out first wins. If you set neither, a
small default is used.

If the budget is spent, the database fails exactly as under :abort: the error
is recorded on db.failure and every later operation raises. The failed writes
are kept on the error.

Set on_error to a function on_error(db, err) and it is called on every
database error — writer or reader — before the policy is applied. Its return
value decides what happens:

return

meaning

:retry or true

retry, within the configured budget

:abort or false

do not retry; fail the database

an Integer

retry at most that many attempts

a Real

retry for at most that many seconds

nothing

use the configured failure policy

The hook receives the Database, so it can inspect the unsaved work with


pending_writes, log the error, alert, or change its mind as an outage
drags on.attempts = Ref(0)
cfg = DatabaseConfig(;
    dbname = "airdb_test", user = "airdb",
    failure = :retry, retry_delay = 0.05,
    on_error = (db, err) -> begin
        attempts[] += 1
        n = length(pending_writes(db))          # the updates a retry would save
        @warn "database error; $n write(s) pending" exception = err
        n > 1000 ? :abort : :retry              # give up if too far behind
    end,
)

A hook can also force a retry even when the configured policy is :abort:cfg = DatabaseConfig(;
    dbname = "airdb_test", user = "airdb",
    failure = :abort,                            # otherwise fail immediately
    on_error = (db, err) -> :retry,              # ... but this hook says retry
)

The budget is per operation

Each flush and each read has its own attempt count and clock. During a long
outage, every read independently retries for up to retry_time before failing,
and the writer’s queue keeps growing until it recovers or gives up.

A Form is an immutable, nested, JSON-able value. Every node in a form tree is a
form: a FormScalar holds a single leaf, a FormContainer holds a
sequence of positional values and a map of symbol-keyed ones, a
VolatileForm (see 

Transactions) holds a form that
persists itself, and a FormExtern (see 

Extern types) holds a
host-level value that is not JSON itself.

A leaf on its own is a form:using AirDB

Form("abc")             # Form("abc")
Form(5)                 # Form(5)
Form(nothing)           # Form(nothing)
value(Form("abc"))      # "abc" — unwrap a scalar form to its leaf

The leaves a form can hold are String, Symbol, Bool, Int64, Float64,
ComplexF64 and Nothing. A narrower scalar is converted where the conversion
cannot lose information:Form(Int32(7))          # Form(7)
Form('x')               # Form("x")
Form(1 + 2im)           # Form(1.0 + 2.0im)
Form(true)              # Form(true) — Bool stays Bool

form(...) builds a container: its positional arguments become the sequence and
its keyword arguments the map.f = form("widget", 1, 2.5, meta = form(name = "abc"))
f                       # Form("widget", 1, 2.5, meta=(name="abc"))

Every value must be a leaf or another form. A Vector or Dict argument
becomes a nested container, so ordinary Julia collections nest naturally:form([1, 2, 3])         # Form((1, 2, 3))
form(Dict(:a => 1))     # Form((a=1))

Form vs. form

Form(x) builds a scalar form from one leaf, and Form(seq, map) builds a
container from prepared collections. form(...) is the general builder, and


to_form converts any value to a form.

How a container is stored

A container’s sequence and map are held in a small, flat, copy-on-write form
while they are small — which is the common case — and promoted to Air’s
persistent structure above a threshold. Every update copies, so a form shared
between two values is never changed under either of them; you never need to know
which representation is in use.

Indexing walks the tree, and a leaf read out of a container is wrapped back into a
scalar form — so every value you read is a form:f = form(10, 20, a = form(x = 1))

f[1]              # Form(10)
value(f[1])       # 10
f[:a]             # Form(x=1)
value(f[:a, :x])  # 1

Use value to get the leaf out of a scalar form.

A form is a collection, so it iterates in one canonical order — every sequence
position, then every map key sorted — and supports the usual tools.f = form(10, 20, a = 30)

length(f)          # 3
isempty(f)         # false
keys(f)            # 1, 2, :a
values(f)          # Form(10), Form(20), Form(30)
pairs(f)           # 1 => Form(10), 2 => Form(20), :a => Form(30)

for (k, v) in f
    # iterates the pairs, in the canonical order
end

Dict(collect(f))   # 1 => Form(10), 2 => Form(20), :a => Form(30)
first(f)           # 1 => Form(10)
last(f)            # :a => Form(30)

copy(f) === f      # true — forms are immutable
empty(f)           # Form() — the empty container

A container carries a held flag, and a symbol scalar form carries the same idea
as a leading quote on its name. hold sets it, unhold clears it, and isheld
tests it. It is part of a form’s value — a held form is not equal to an unheld one
— and it is written in the form’s JSON, so a held form round-trips through the
database.h = hold(form(a = 1))        # the same form, now held
isheld(h)                    # true
hold(h) === h                # idempotent

hold(Form(:abc))             # Form(Symbol("'abc")) — a leading quote
hold(Form(Symbol("'abc")))   # unchanged — quotes do not stack
unhold(Form(Symbol("'abc"))) # Form(:abc)

hold(Form(5))                # Form(5) — other forms are returned unchanged

A symbol that begins with a colon is a keyword, and a keyword is a different,
inert leaf: holding one is the keyword, so hold and unhold leave it exactly as
it is, and isheld does not count it as held.hold(Form(Symbol(":abc")))     # unchanged — a keyword is inert
unhold(Form(Symbol(":abc")))   # unchanged — a keyword never unholds
isheld(Form(Symbol(":abc")))   # false — a keyword is not a held symbol
Form(Symbol(":abc"))           # not equal to Form(Symbol("'abc"))

Every update returns a new form; the original is untouched. (setindex here is
Air’s persistent verb, not Base.setindex!.)g = form(1, 2, 3)

setindex(g, 9, 1)      # Form(9, 2, 3)
push(g, 4)             # Form(1, 2, 3, 4)
pop(g)                 # Form(1, 2)
delete(g, 2)           # Form(1, 3)   — items shift down; no blanks
setindex(form(a = 1), 2, :b)   # Form(a=1, b=2)

g                      # Form(1, 2, 3) — unchanged

An integer index equal to one past the end of the sequence appends:setindex(g, 4, 4)      # Form(1, 2, 3, 4)
setindex(g, 9, 5)      # ERROR: BoundsError

to_form converts any value to a form: a form is returned as it is, a leaf
becomes a FormScalar, and a collection becomes a container.to_form(5)             # Form(5)
to_form("abc")         # Form("abc")
to_form(nothing)       # Form(nothing)
to_form([1, 2, 3])     # Form(1, 2, 3)
to_form(Dict(:a => 1)) # Form(a=1)

Two forms are equal when they are the same kind of form with equal contents
(numeric leaves compare as numbers, so Form(5) == Form(5.0)). A nested
container prints without the Form prefix, so a form reads like a call:form(1, 2) == form(1, 2)               # true
form(b = 1, a = 2)                     # Form(a=2, b=1) — keys print sorted
sprint(show, form("a", b = 1))         # "Form(\"a\", b=1)"
sprint(show, Form(5))                  # "Form(5)"

A container is written as the three-element list [seq, map, held], and a scalar
form as its bare leaf, which makes the format self-describing. Strings and symbols are
both JSON strings, told apart by the first character inside the quotes (' for a
string, : for a symbol); a float always carries a point or exponent; and a
complex number is written as {"re": …, "im": …}.using AirDB: to_JSON, from_JSON

to_JSON(form("widget", 1, 2.5))   # "[[\"'widget\", 1, 2.5], {}, false]"
to_JSON(hold(form(a = 1)))        # "[[], {\":a\": 1}, true]" — the flag is last
to_JSON(Form(5))                  # "5"
to_JSON(Form("abc"))              # "\"'abc\""

from_JSON("[[\"'widget\", 1, 2.5], {}]") == form("widget", 1, 2.5)   # true
from_JSON("5") == Form(5)         # true — a bare scalar is a scalar form
from_JSON("{\":a\": 1}")          # Form(a=1) — a bare object is a map-only form

A form may link to a VolatileForm, written "@<uuid>". Reading such a link
needs the database that owns it (see 

Persistence); without one
it is an error.

A form may also hold a FormExtern, written as the tagged list ["extern", "<type>", <payload>]. See 

Extern types.from_JSON("[[\"@11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111\"], {}]")
# ERROR: a form link (@...) needs a Database to be resolved

AirDB depends on 

Air.jl 0.2 and


LibPQ.jl. Add it to a project with:using Pkg
Pkg.add("AirDB")            # once AirDB is registered

AirDB never creates or manages a PostgreSQL server — it connects to one you
provide. For experimenting, the repository ships a docker-compose.yml that
starts a throwaway server:docker compose up -d        # postgres:16 on localhost:5432, user/db "airdb"

Everything AirDB needs to reach the server goes in a DatabaseConfig. The
structured fields cover the common case; you can also hand it a libpq URI or
connection string, which is used verbatim.using AirDB

cfg = DatabaseConfig(;
    host     = "localhost",
    port     = 5432,
    dbname   = "airdb_test",
    user     = "airdb",
    password = "airdb",
)# ... or a libpq URL / connection string:
cfg = DatabaseConfig("postgresql://airdb:airdb@localhost:5432/airdb_test")
cfg = DatabaseConfig("host=localhost port=5432 dbname=airdb_test user=airdb")

Other fields tune behaviour — pool size, write batching, and what to do on
failure. See 

Failures and retries and 

Persistence.cfg = DatabaseConfig(;
    dbname       = "airdb_test",
    user         = "airdb",
    readpoolsize = 16,      # connections kept for reads
    max_batch    = 1,       # commits accumulated before one database write
    failure      = :abort,  # or :retry
)

There are two constructors. create_database initializes a new AirDB
database — it creates the tables — and returns a Database. open_database
connects to one that already exists.db = create_database(cfg)            # create the tables and connect
# ... work with db ...
close(db)

db = open_database(cfg)              # connect to an existing AirDB database

Pass overwrite = true to create_database to drop and recreate the AirDB
tables first — convenient while experimenting, never what you want in
production.db = create_database(cfg; overwrite = true)

Opening a database that has no AirDB schema raises an ArgumentError telling you
to create one.

A VolatileForm holds a Form and has a stable UUID. Its positional arguments
become the form’s sequence and its keyword arguments its map, exactly as for
Form.widget = VolatileForm(db, "widget", n = 1, tags = ["a", "b"])

Reading a form is ordinary indexing. The body is read from the database the first
time it is needed.widget[]        # Form("widget", n=1, tags=("a", "b"))
value(widget[:n]) # 1
widget[:tags]   # Form("a", "b") — a nested collection is a nested form

Writing must happen inside an Air transaction; the change is staged during the
transaction and sent to the writer when it commits.@tx widget[:n] = 42
AirDB.sync(db)  # block until the writer has saved everything sent so far
value(widget[:n]) # 42

AirDB.sync is the way to wait for durability: because the writer is sequential,
once it has processed the sync message every earlier write is on disk. In a
server you usually do not call sync after every write — the write is queued
and saved asynchronously.

For tests that should not depend on PostgreSQL, MemoryDatabase() builds a fake,
in-memory database with the same surface — VolatileForm, named_form,
get_form, sync — that saves nothing and keeps no history.db = MemoryDatabase()
vf = VolatileForm(db, n = 1)
@tx vf[:n] = 2
AirDB.sync(db)
value(vf[:n])          # 2

close(db) flushes any queued writes and closes every connection. Further
operations on a closed database raise.close(db)

Read-your-writes

Within one Database, a read always sees the latest committed value, even if the
writer has not yet reached the database: the form is cached in memory and the
pending write keeps it alive. sync is only needed when another process — or a
later session — must see the write.

A PostgreSQL-backed persistence layer built on


Air.jl’s software transactional memory.

AirDB lets you keep shared application state in memory as ordinary Julia objects
and have every committed change written to PostgreSQL automatically, in
transaction order, without locks in your own code. It is aimed at asynchronous,
multithreaded servers whose threads share data and whose write order matters.

Air provides three building blocks:

a Volatile, a Ref-like cell that may only be written inside a
transaction and is guaranteed constant for the duration of one;

an Actor, a worker with its own thread and message queue, which runs sent
functions one at a time; and

transactions (@tx / tx), which make a group of reads, writes, and sends
take effect all at once or not at all, re-running the body if another thread
interferes.

AirDB builds three objects on top of those:

Form — an immutable, JSON-able nested map/sequence structure, the value
type that gets stored;

VolatileForm — a Form with a stable UUID that writes itself to the
database when the transaction that changed it commits; and

Database — the connection, the single writer actor, the read pool, and a
cache of live forms.

One writer, many readers

Every Database owns one writer actor. Committed updates are sent to it in
Air’s global commit order and written by it in that order, so the database never
sees two writers race. Reads go through a separate pool of connections and never
wait on the writer.

using AirDB
using Air            # for the @tx / tx transaction macros

cfg = DatabaseConfig(; host = "localhost", dbname = "airdb", user = "airdb")
db = create_database(cfg; overwrite = true)   # initialize a new AirDB database

widget = VolatileForm(db, "widget", n = 1)    # a new form, persisted on commit

@tx widget[:n] = 42                           # change it inside a transaction
AirDB.sync(db)                                # wait until the writer has saved it
value(widget[:n])                              # 42

The value lives in memory and in PostgreSQL. Another process (or another
connection) can read it back by its UUID:id = widget.id
close(db)
db = open_database(cfg)
r = get_form(db, id)      # a fresh handle; the body is read lazily
value(r[:n])               # 42

Getting started — configuring a connection and
creating or opening a database.

Named forms — giving a form a name like "root" so it can
be found without a UUID.

Forms — building, reading, updating, and encoding forms.

Transactions and volatile forms — how writes commit.

Indexing and updating — the path-based access paradigm.

Persistence — the schema, lazy loading, the cache, and
batching.

Concurrency — many threads, one writer.

Failures and retries — what happens when PostgreSQL is
unreachable.

API reference — the exported names at a glance.

AirDB requires Julia 1.10 or later, 

Air.jl
0.2, and a PostgreSQL server you provide (the library never manages the server
itself). The repository ships a docker-compose.yml that starts a throwaway
PostgreSQL 16 for the tests and the examples in this book.

Forms are navigated with a path of keys. The same indexing works on any form,
and a VolatileForm met along the way is transparent — its value is used in its
place — which makes a tree of forms read like a single nested value.

An Integer is a sequence position; a Symbol is a map key.

A vector key (or :, meaning every key) fans out, building a new form
over the selection.

A value read out of a container is wrapped back into a form, so indexing always
yields a form: a leaf comes back as a FormScalar, which 

value
unwraps. The value at the final key is returned as it is, so a final
VolatileForm comes back whole rather than expanded.

f = form(10, 20, a = form(x = 1, y = 2), b = form(x = 3))

f[1]              # Form(10)
value(f[1])       # 10
f[:a]             # Form(x=1, y=2)
value(f[:a, :x])  # 1   — same as value(f[:a][:x])

A VolatileForm is transparent when you index through it, but returned whole
when it is the final value:a = VolatileForm(db, x = 0)
b = VolatileForm(db, x = 1)
fv = form(a = a, b = b)

fv[:a]            # the VolatileForm itself
value(fv[:a, :x]) # 0    — fv[:a] was dereferenced to reach :x
value(fv[:a][:x]) # 0

A vector key builds a form over the selection. Because reading extracts data,
volatiles are eliminated from whatever it builds — a VolatileForm in the result
is replaced by its value.f[[:a, :b], :x]        # Form(a=1, b=3)
f[[:a, :b], [:x]]      # Form(a=Form(x=1), b=Form(x=3)) — a nested level per vector
f[2:3]                 # Form(20, 30) — a range is a vector key, so it fans out

A range over the sequence’s own collection gives the subsequence, as a sequence
rather than a plain Vector, so it can be used as a container’s sequence:f.seq[2:3]             # the FormSeq holding 20 and 30

With volatiles in the tree:g = form(a = VolatileForm(db, x = 0), b = VolatileForm(db, x = 1))

g[[:a, :b], :x]        # Form(a=0, b=1)          — the volatiles are eliminated
g[[:a, :b], [:x]]      # Form(a=Form(x=0), b=Form(x=1))

: selects every sequence position and every map key:h = form(form(x = 10), form(x = 20), a = form(x = 30))
h[:, :x]               # Form(10, 20, a=30)

A missing key raises. get supplies a default for a missing final key; a
missing intermediate key still raises.f[:z]                          # ERROR: KeyError: key :z not found
get(f, :z, :none)              # :none
get(f, :a, :z, :none)          # :none   — :a exists, :z does not
get(f, :z, :x, :none)          # ERROR: KeyError — the intermediate :z is missing

setindex builds a new form and never writes a volatile. A volatile on the
update path is therefore eliminated (replaced by its plain, updated value);
volatiles off the path are kept as links.setindex(f, 99, :a, :x)        # Form(10, 20, a=Form(x=99, y=2), b=Form(x=3))
setindex(f, 5, 1)              # Form(5, 20, a=..., b=...)
setindex(f, 42, :c)            # adds a new key
setindex(f, 4, 4)              # appends: Form(10, 20, ..., 4)r = setindex(g, 99, :a, :x)
r[:a]                          # Form(x=99) — a plain container; the volatile is gone
r[:b] === g[:b]                # true       — the off-path volatile is kept

A fan-out setindex returns a form over the selection:setindex(f, 99, [:a, :b], :x)  # Form(a=Form(x=99, y=2), b=Form(x=99))

setindex! walks the path and writes the deepest VolatileForm on it — the
last volatile among the values along the path, including the final one. It
rebuilds that volatile along the keys below it. If no value on the path is a
volatile, it raises, because a persistent form cannot be mutated.@tx g[:a, :x] = 5              # writes the volatile g[:a]; reads g

Because it writes a volatile, setindex! must run inside a transaction. Setting
the final key sets the final volatile’s value:@tx g[:a] = form(x = 42)       # sets the value of the volatile at :a

A fan-out writes each branch’s target:@tx g[[:a, :b], :x] = 9        # writes both volatiles

An integer one past the end of a sequence appends:seq = VolatileForm(db, 1, 2)
@tx seq[3] = 3                 # seq[] == Form(1, 2, 3)

Writes are not local

setindex! writes the deepest volatile, which may be shared with other
structures, so the change is visible everywhere that volatile is reachable. This
is the intended model — volatiles are identity objects — but it means the effect
of g[:a, 1] = x is not always obvious from the call site.

map returns a form with the same keys, every immediate value replaced by
fn(value). A VolatileForm value is handed to fn as the VolatileForm
object, so the function decides whether to keep or drop it. If the form itself is
a VolatileForm, the function is applied to its value; if it is a FormScalar,
it is applied to the leaf.map(x -> x * 2, form(1, 2, a = 3))     # Form(2, 4, a=6)
map(x -> x + 1, Form(5))               # Form(6)
map(identity, fv)                      # same keys; the volatiles are passed through
map(v -> v isa VolatileForm ? v[] : v, fv)   # ... or expanded, if you prefer

The functional verbs push, pop, and delete likewise operate on a
VolatileForm’s value and return a new form; they never write the volatile.push(seq, 9)       # a new form
delete(seq, 1)     # a new form with items shifted down

Beyond get/setindex, a form is operated on with the usual functional verbs.
Each value handed to a function is passed as a form.f = form(10, 20, a = form(x = 1), b = 3)

update(f, v -> value(v) + 1, :a, :x)   # read-modify-write: Form(10, 20, a=(x=2), b=3)
update!(vf, v -> value(v) + 1, :n)     # ... transactional: deepest volatile, like setindex!

merge(form(a = 1), form(b = 2))        # Form(a=1, b=2)
merge(form(a = 1), form(a = 9))        # Form(a=9) — the later form wins
merge_with((x, y) -> value(x) + value(y), form(a = 1), form(a = 2))   # Form(a=3)

haskey(f, :a, :x)                      # true — haskey takes a path
select_keys(f, [:b, :a])               # Form(b=3, a=(x=1)); missing keys are skipped

filter(v -> v isa FormScalar && value(v) isa Int64, form(1, "s", a = 2))  # Form(1, a=2)
map_values(v -> value(v) + 1, form(1, a = 2))   # Form(2, a=3)
map_keys(k -> Symbol("k_", k), form(a = 1))     # Form(k_a=1)
deep_map(v -> ..., f)                            # transform every node, bottom-up

to_vector(form(1, 2, 3))   # [1, 2, 3]
to_dict(form(a = 1))       # Dict(:a => 1)

update and the other verbs without a ! are purely functional; update! writes
the deepest VolatileForm on the path and raises if there is none — the same
rule as setindex! — so it must run inside a transaction.

A project usually has a few well-known forms — a "root" holding shared
data, a "settings" form, a per-user entry point. Rather than pass UUIDs around,
give a form a name.

A name is just an alias: it lives in a form_name table, and the form it
points to still has its own UUID and its own rows in form_history and
form_current. The table is small, so a Database keeps it in memory as a
PDict{String,VolatileForm} — and, because names are almost always changed inside
a transaction, that PDict lives in an Air Volatile. A change to it is
therefore transactional: it commits with the surrounding transaction (or in one of
its own) and is retried or discarded with it, just like the form data, while the
database write is scheduled through the writer in the same commit.

hierarchy.lvl2: Looking a form up by name
Looking a form up by name

records.content:
named_form looks a name up. A name may be a Symbol or a String — both refer
to the same form, because a name is compared by its string value.

create decides what happens when the name is not found:

create

name found

name not found

false (the default)

return the form

raise

true

raise

create a new named form and return it

nothing

return the form

return nothingusing AirDB

named_form(db, "root")                    # ERROR if "root" is not registered
named_form(db, "root"; create = nothing)  # nothing if it is not registered
named_form(db, :root; create = nothing)   # Symbol and String agree

With create = true, a new form is created and registered when the name is free:root = named_form(db, "root"; create = true, value = form(version = 1))
named_form(db, "root") === root         # true
named_form(db, "root"; create = true)   # ERROR: the name "root" is already in use

The value argument is the new form’s initial value, used only when a form is
created. It may be:

a Form — used as-is;

anything a form can be made from, such as a number — converted, so 5 becomes
Form(5);

no value (the default) — an empty container;

an existing VolatileForm — in which case no new form is made, and the name
is simply pointed at the given form.named_form(db, "a"; create = true, value = form(x = 1))  # holds Form(x=1)
named_form(db, "b"; create = true, value = 5)            # holds Form(5)
named_form(db, "c"; create = true)                       # holds an empty container

shared = VolatileForm(db, n = 1)
named_form(db, "d"; create = true, value = shared)       # aliases `shared`
named_form(db, "d") === shared                           # true — the same object

name_form! registers a form under a name, overwriting whatever was there:name_form!(db, "current", some_form)
name_form!(db, "current", another_form)   # now points at another_form

named_forms returns the whole table as a PDict{String,VolatileForm}. A PDict
is immutable, so the result is safe to share and to keep; each value is a
(possibly not-yet-loaded) VolatileForm.names = named_forms(db)
names["root"]           # the form named "root"
haskey(names, "settings")

The table is loaded when a database is opened, so another process — or a later
session — finds the same names.close(db)
db = open_database(cfg)
value(named_form(db, "root")[:version])   # 1

The name table is a Volatile, so registering or renaming a form is
transactional. named_form with create = true and name_form! join the
caller’s transaction if there is one, and otherwise run in a transaction of their
own — so you can call them anywhere.

Inside a transaction, the registration commits with everything else:@tx begin
    root = named_form(db, "root"; create = true, value = form(version = 1))
    root[:version] = 2                  # both commit together
end

and, just as importantly, it is discarded if the transaction does not commit:try
    @tx begin
        named_form(db, "temp"; create = true)
        error("abort")
    end
catch
end
named_form(db, "temp"; create = nothing)   # nothing — the registration never happened

Reading the table inside a transaction registers a read of it, so a transaction
that looks a name up is retried if another transaction changes the table — the
same optimistic rule that governs everything else in Air.

Two transactions that register names at once are serialized by Air’s conflict
detection, so the table stays consistent without any lock of our own.

AirDB keeps two tables: an append-only history and an up-to-date snapshot.CREATE TABLE form_history (
    form_id     UUID        NOT NULL,
    version     BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),
    tx_id       BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    payload     JSONB       NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (form_id, version)
);

CREATE TABLE form_current (
    form_id     UUID        PRIMARY KEY,
    version     BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),
    payload     JSONB       NOT NULL
);

-- An alias table for well-known forms (see Named forms).
CREATE TABLE form_name (
    name        TEXT        PRIMARY KEY,
    form_id     UUID        NOT NULL REFERENCES form_current(form_id)
);

Every committed update appends a new row to form_history and upserts
form_current, in one database transaction. Reads fetch exclusively from
form_current, so a lookup is an indexed point read by form_id. The version is
assigned by the database (1 on the first insert, one more each time), and tx_id
groups the rows written by a single commit.db = create_database(cfg; overwrite = true)
vf = VolatileForm(db, "widget", n = 1)
AirDB.sync(db)

@tx vf[:n] = 2
AirDB.sync(db)
# form_current:  version = 2
# form_history:  (version 1, tx_id 1), (version 2, tx_id 2)

A form is identified by its UUID. get_form(db, id) returns the live form if it
is still in memory, and otherwise a fresh handle whose body is read from the
database the first time it is needed.id = vf.id
get_form(db, id) === vf          # true — the same object while it is alive
AirDB.isloaded(get_form(db, id)) # true

# drop every reference and collect: the cache releases it
vf = nothing
GC.gc(); GC.gc()

r = get_form(db, id)
AirDB.isloaded(r)                # false — only the id is known so far
value(r[:n])                      # 2     — the body is loaded from PostgreSQL here

The cache holds each form through a WeakRef, so it never keeps a form alive on
its own: a form stays cached exactly as long as something else references it, and
is released back to the database once nothing does. The same id always yields the
same object within one Database, which is what keeps Air’s transactional reads
on a form coherent across threads.

A form may hold another VolatileForm. It is stored as the string "@<uuid>",
never expanded, so a form that links to itself — or in a cycle — still encodes.child  = VolatileForm(db, v = 1)
parent = VolatileForm(db, name = "parent", kid = child)
AirDB.sync(db)

AirDB.to_JSON(parent[])
# "[[], {\":kid\": \"@<uuid-of-child>\", \":name\": \"'parent\"}]"

Reading the parent loads only the parent; the child is loaded when it is touched.parent[:kid]            # the child VolatileForm — not expanded
value(parent[:kid][:v])  # 1 — now the child is loaded

Because loading a form never expands the forms it links to, loading a parent does
not pull in the whole database, and cyclic references are handled without
recursion.

By default each commit is written as soon as the writer receives it. Setting
max_batch lets the writer accumulate several commits and write them in one
database transaction — useful under heavy load.bcfg = DatabaseConfig(; dbname = "airdb_test", user = "airdb", max_batch = 3)
bdb = create_database(bcfg; overwrite = true)

bf = VolatileForm(bdb, n = 0)
AirDB.sync(bdb)

@tx bf[:n] = 1
@tx bf[:n] = 2                  # fewer than max_batch: not written yet ...
value(bf[:n])                    # 2 — ... but the in-memory value is current
@tx bf[:n] = 3                  # the third fills the batch; it is written at once
AirDB.sync(bdb)                 # sync flushes a partial batch too

Read-your-writes still holds

While a batch is waiting, the forms in it are pinned by the writer’s queue, so a
lookup is a cache hit rather than a database read. You always see the latest
committed value in-process, even before it reaches the database.

A VolatileForm is a thin wrapper around an Air Volatile{Form}. It can be read
at any time, but it may only be written inside a transaction, and when that
transaction commits, the new value is sent to the database’s writer.

using AirDB, Air

widget = VolatileForm(db, "widget", n = 1)

@tx widget[:n] = 42       # stage the change ...
# ... it commits here, and the writer is told to save the new form
value(widget[:n])          # 42

Outside a transaction a write is an error, inherited from Air:widget[:n] = 5
# ERROR: cannot set volatile outside of transaction

The tx function is the non-macro form, handy when you already have a closure:tx(() -> (widget[:n] = value(widget[:n]) + 1))

All the writes in one transaction become visible together, and all the sends are
dispatched together, in commit order. A commit that changes several forms writes
them to the database in a single database transaction, so a reader never sees
half of a commit.a = VolatileForm(db, kind = "A")
b = VolatileForm(db, kind = "B")

@tx begin
    a[:v] = 1
    b[:v] = 2
end
AirDB.sync(db)
(value(a[:v]), value(b[:v]))   # (1, 2) — both landed together

hierarchy.lvl2: The body may run more than once
The body may run more than once

records.content:
Air is optimistic: a transaction records what it reads, and if any of those
values change before it commits, the transaction is discarded and re-run. So the
body of a transaction must be free of side effects other than the transactional
ones.# Good: the only side effect is the transactional write.
@tx widget[:n] = value(widget[:n]) + 1

# Bad: this prints a different number of times depending on contention.
@tx begin
    println("attempt")          # do not do this
    widget[:n] = value(widget[:n]) + 1
end

If the body throws, nothing is written:try
    @tx begin
        widget[:n] = 99
        error("abort")
    end
catch
end
value(widget[:n])                 # still 42 — the write never happened

hierarchy.lvl2: How a write reaches the database
How a write reaches the database

records.content:
AirDB intercepts the write, and — once, per transaction — arranges for the
committed values to reach the writer actor. Air guarantees that a message sent
during a transaction is dispatched only if the transaction commits, and in
commit order. So the database sees exactly the transactions that succeeded, in
the order they committed, and a retried transaction never leaves a trace.

What this means for you

You never call the writer directly, and you never write to the database by hand.
Write forms inside @tx, and AirDB does the rest. Use AirDB.sync(db) only when
something outside the process needs to observe the write.

Reading a form inside a transaction registers an Air read, so the transaction
sees a consistent value and will be re-run if it changes. A form that has not yet
been loaded from the database is loaded on first access — that is ordinary lazy
loading (see 

Persistence), and it is safe to do inside a
transaction.@tx begin
    current = value(widget[:n])   # read (and register)
    widget[:n] = current + 1 # write
end

hierarchy.lvl2: Volatile forms link to one another
Volatile forms link to one another

records.content:
Because a form may hold a VolatileForm, forms compose into a tree of
independently-versioned pieces. A transaction that reaches through a child form
reads it and (if it writes) writes only the part it actually changes; see


Indexing and updating for the details.child  = VolatileForm(db, n = 0)
parent = VolatileForm(db, name = "parent", child = child)

@tx parent[:child, :n] = 1     # writes `child`, reads `parent`
